text:
Most people I talk to can name about half the devices on their home wifi.

The laptop, the phones, the TV. After that it gets vague. And a home network today usually has more on it than people expect: the security camera you set up years ago and never updated, the smart plug running firmware nobody at the vendor has touched since, the printer quietly serving a web admin page with the default password still on it.

None of that is exotic. It's just invisible. The device works, so you stop thinking about it, and meanwhile it sits on the same network as your banking tabs.

This is the whole reason I built NetVane. It finds every device, tells you what each one is, and checks what they're exposing against a bundled vulnerability database, then says in plain language what's actually worth fixing. Not a wall of CVE numbers. Something closer to "this camera has a known exploited flaw, here's the firmware page."

You can do a lot of this by hand if you enjoy reading ARP tables. Most people don't, and that's fine. But "I have no idea what's on my network" shouldn't be the normal state of things.

If you want to see what's on yours, the free edition does the discovery and CVE matching with no account and no trial clock: netvane.doorvane.com

The feature I'm most proud of in NetVane is basically an admission that you shouldn't trust me.

When you build a privacy tool, you spend a lot of time saying "it's local, nothing leaves your machine, no cloud." The problem is every other tool says exactly the same words, and there's no way for a normal person to tell the honest ones from the ones that are quietly lying. The claim is invisible. You either believe the marketing or you don't.

That bothered me. So NetVane has a ledger built into the app that logs every internet connection it makes, with what, when, and why. Run a scan and watch it: it stays empty, because scanning your network only ever talks to your own devices. The one time anything shows up is when you ask it to check for a vulnerability-data update, and it tells you that's what it's doing.

It would have been much easier to write "we respect your privacy" on the website and move on. But I don't want you to take my word for it. I'd rather you check once, see for yourself, and then forget about it.

Verifiable beats promised. That's the one idea the whole thing is built around.

The most common reaction I get to NetVane is "isn't this just Fing?"

Fair. There are already good network scanners. Fing, Angry IP Scanner, Advanced IP Scanner, I've used all of them. If you just want a list of what's connected, they do that well and several are free.

Here's where NetVane is genuinely different, and where it isn't.

It isn't different at the "find the devices" layer. Anyone can list IPs and MAC addresses.

It is different at the next step. It takes the open ports and service versions it finds and matches them against a vulnerability database bundled inside the app, then tells you what's actually exploitable versus just open. An open port isn't a problem. An open port running a service with a known exploited CVE is. Most scanners stop before that line.

The other difference is where your data goes. Some of those tools phone home. NetVane doesn't, and it shows you a live ledger of every request it makes so you can confirm that rather than take my word for it.

If you already have a scanner you're happy with, honestly, keep it. But if you've ever looked at a list of open ports and thought "okay, but which of these actually matters," that gap is the reason NetVane exists.
